stem:
A 29-year-old with type 1 diabetes wants to stop contraception this month. Her HbA1c is 94 mmol/mol (10.8%), with frequent high glucose readings but no recent severe hypoglycaemia. Renal and retinal assessments are being arranged; she has started appropriate folate and is taking no teratogenic medicine. Her GP and diabetes team discuss pregnancy planning.

Which recommendation best addresses her current risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Try to conceive now, since folate has started and insulin can be adjusted
options.explanation: Folate does not offset the congenital-anomaly and miscarriage risk of an HbA1c of 94 mmol/mol at conception; organogenesis occurs before insulin could be adjusted.

options.label: B
options.text: Try to conceive once renal and retinal assessments are reported normal
options.explanation: Normal renal and retinal assessments are important, but they do not address the glycaemic risk to the fetus.

options.label: C
options.text: Proceed now with early specialist review and a first-trimester scan
options.explanation: Early review and scans detect problems but do not reduce the anomaly risk set by glucose control at conception.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue contraception while improving glucose control before conception
options.explanation: An HbA1c this high carries a substantial anomaly risk, so effective contraception should continue while control is improved towards the pre-conception target before trying to conceive.

options.label: E
options.text: Continue contraception until her HbA1c is below 10%, then conceive
options.explanation: An HbA1c above about 10% (86 mmol/mol) is the level at which pregnancy should be avoided, not the target; conception should wait until HbA1c is as close as safely possible to 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or below.

context: For markedly raised HbA1c in pre-existing diabetes, improve glycaemic control before conception rather than relying on later screening to manage the risk.
